The work adds a two-story restaurant barn beside the pond, a dedicated wedding and events venue overlooking the vineyard, a pool with patio and bar where the parking lot used to be, and a 35-room hotel expansion with six walk-out suites. Six building types on one site, sited so the property still reads as a working farm rather than a resort. Medical Office Complex Ridgewood Drive, Bangor, Maine — Medical Office A 12,500 square foot single-story medical office building planned as four tenant suites on Bangor's Ridgewood Drive medical corridor. The site is wooded and undeveloped, with no municipal sewer — so parking, septic field, setbacks, and building footprint all draw from the same fixed acreage. The site plan was solved before the floor plan was. Sugarloaf Mountain Home Carrabassett Valley, Maine — Residential A 4,000 square foot four-season home on a lot adjacent to a new ski trail spur at Sugarloaf, with a double-height living room, indoor-outdoor fireplace, and a master suite above. Most of the glass faces northwest — the coldest wall in western Maine, and the only direction with a view of the Carrabassett Valley and the Bigelow Range. The house is tucked into the mountainside and oriented for solar gain east and west. Downtown Office Renovation Bangor, Maine — Adaptive Reuse + Commercial Office A 10,000 square foot gut renovation of a 19th-century brick warehouse across from Penobscot Plaza, a block off the Penobscot River. New elevator, new egress stairs, expanded conference rooms, and offices rebuilt for daylight and circulation. All original windows are being replaced with Marvin direct glaze, the envelope waterproofed, and the brick sealed for the first time. Contemporary 4 Bedroom Gulf Coast Residence Gulf Coast, Florida — Residential A 7,500 square foot four-bedroom house designed for the Florida Gulf Coast — two stories under standing seam metal, deep covered balconies on both levels, full-height glass to the living volumes, a three-car garage, and a pool terrace. title: Ideas & Blog | Architecture Insights from Ervin Architecture
text: Ideas & Blog | Architecture Insights from Ervin Architecture Skip to content Work Featured Projects Project Index Current Projects About EA About Us Our Methodology Our Process Press & Awards Blog Work Featured Projects Project Index Current Projects About EA About Us Our Methodology Our Process Press & Awards Blog Contact Us Ervin Architecture Blog Discover the Insights, Ideas, and Trends Shaping Tomorrow's Designs Ideas Elevating Fan Experience: Suites, Clubs & VIP Design in Modern Music Venues In today’s live entertainment landscape, premium and VIP offerings are not a luxury—they’re the business model. Suites, sky decks, and club levels help venues compete for tours, support capital improvements, and give fans new ways to connect with the artists they love. Read More Ideas How Small Cities Can Attract Big Tours: Designing Music Venues for Regional Impact Big tours used to belong almost exclusively to major metros. But over the last decade, smaller cities have started landing A-list acts and multi-night runs that would have been unthinkable a generation ago. The secret is rarely just better marketing. It’s almost always better venues. Read More Ideas Designing Restaurants for the Rhythm of Live Entertainment At Ervin Architecture, we’ve designed both major venues and destination restaurants that live in the same orbit, like KANU in Old Town and projects connected with the Maine Savings Amphitheater in Bangor. Here’s how we think about restaurant design in the context of live entertainment. Read More Ideas From Mill Towns to Nightlife Destinations: Adaptive Reuse for Restaurants & Clubs Across North America, smaller cities and former mill towns are sitting on a quiet superpower: historic building stock. Brick warehouses, timber-framed mercantile structures, and century-old storefronts often sit underused while communities search for ways to bring people—and energy—back downtown. Read More Ideas Rooftop Bars, Sky Decks & Premium Terraces: Designing Elevated Hospitality Experiences Rooftop spaces have quietly become some of the most powerful revenue-generating real estate in hospitality and live entertainment. A great rooftop bar or sky deck can turn a “nice venue” into the place everyone wants to be seen. The design of Kanù pays tribute to Old Town Canoe, a business that was owned and operated by the client’s family for many years. Our team crafted a dynamic and versatile space that encompasses a farm-to-table restaurant on the first floor, a vibrant nightclub on the second floor, and a breathtaking rooftop lounge on the third floor. Kanù is an unforgettable experience for visitors, combining exceptional dining, lively entertainment, and stunning views. This 3-story multi-functional complex reflects our commitment to design excellence and establishes itself as a must-visit destination in Maine. As part of an adaptive reuse economic initiative in the City of Old Town, Maine and the client’s vision of revitalizing his home town into an Arts & Entertainment District. The project involved transforming a 19th-century brick and timber mercantile building into the anchor tenant for the downtown district. By repurposing the existing building and incorporating historical elements with contemporary aesthetics, Kanù was able to attract visitors to the area, generate new jobs, and add cultural vibrancy. Our connections to Old Town Canoe inspired the name KANÙ. Alex Gray Owner + Restaurateur Designing a Farm-to-Table Restaurant in Old Town, Maine Before Design The building arrived as a failing structure, which meant the work started with assessment rather than renderings — what the building could still do, and what it would cost to make it do more. The bones were typical of 19th-century masonry construction: reinforced timber floor joists, a few iron columns, tongue and groove hardwood floors. Buildings like this were built to carry freight, so the structure was sound. What sat on top of it was era-specific cheap infill, and decades of economic stagnation meant almost none of it had been touched. Bringing a building like this back starts with gut demolition of everything but the original structure. That resets the typology and lets the architect address the things that decide whether the building can hold people at all — egress, fire separation, structural reinforcement for floor deflection, acoustics, universal access, fire suppression. Function comes before flavor. Only once those were solved could the design turn to what the room would feel like. Governing Concepts Four requirements shaped the plan before anything else. Two means of egress. Separate and distinct exits on every floor, with travel distances and signage that work when a full house needs to leave at once. Fully sprinklered. Complete coverage throughout — supply, heads, piping, valves — in a building that had none. Fire separation between floors. Fire-rated assemblies at every floor line, so three venues can operate simultaneously without one compromising the others. Kitchen exhaust. Two kitchens on the ground floor, one conventional and one solid fuel, each with its own ventilation requirements for smoke, grease, and odor. The Ground Floor The restaurant is a 150-seat assembly space designed for family dining, with a bar and two bathrooms placed for accessibility rather than convenience. Behind it sits the working half of the floor. Conventional kitchen — standard appliances and equipment for the farm-to-table menu: workstations, cooking ranges, ovens, refrigeration, and the fixtures that go with them. Solid fuel grill kitchen — a separate kitchen dedicated to cooking over a solid fuel source, with its own ventilation and specialized equipment. A Le Panyol wood-fired oven and a Grillworks wood-fired grill, with the oven surround by Maine Wood Heat. Solid fuel cooking carries different code requirements than a conventional line, and the two kitchens were designed and ventilated as separate systems. Wait staff area — a work zone for serving trays, POS systems, and the supplies service runs on. Walk-in refrigeration — storage for perishables, ingredients, and stock. Laundry room — dedicated space for the restaurant’s linen and uniform cleaning. At the front, a lobby handles the transition from the street into the restaurant, and a greeting area with seating gives waiting guests somewhere to be. The layout came from the site as much as from the program. Buildings abut Kanù on both sides, so natural light, utilities, and ventilation all had to come from the front or the rear. Utility entrances came in off Main Street. The rear was the only place kitchen exhaust could go — so the kitchen went to the rear, which kept the street-facing facade intact. The rear datum also sits higher than the front, which required a ramped approach for accessible entry. Bathrooms were pushed toward the rear, landing at a midpoint in the plan. Universal design was the standard throughout: anywhere an able-bodied guest can go, a guest in a wheelchair can go. Midway through schematic design the client acquired the buildings on either side, which added an elevator and turned three separate structures into one interconnected complex. Materials The dining room is broken into zones — privacy where it’s wanted, openness where it isn’t. Sweeping ceiling elements move the room away from a rectilinear box and tie the zones together. The entry sets the tone with an antique lectern from Soll’s in Canaan. Custom velvet furniture and pieces by Kellex give the room weight. The hardwood flooring was salvaged from the building next door. Interlam wall coverings, Plyboo bamboo soffits, and Tilebar tile carry the texture. Reclaimed timber from Maine Heritage Timber and masonry work by Pat Manley Masonry. CNC fabrication came out of the University of Maine’s Material Science Lab. Architectural lighting by Greg Day Lighting — old-world fixtures with warm hues and intricate detail, placed to pick out the building’s features rather than flatten them. Restored brick runs behind all of it — cleaned, repaired, and left visible, so the 19th-century building stays present in a contemporary room rather than being covered over. Familiar materials, reinterpreted: wood, stone, and metal in contemporary forms against a structure that predates all of it. Timeline The client approached Ervin Architecture in 2017 for renderings of a three-venue vision — restaurant, nightclub, rooftop lounge. Those renderings secured the building. Construction ran into the pandemic. Supply chains, costs, and crew safety all had to be managed while the work continued.
